body.heading: A race against decay
paragraphs: For a creature to fossilise, it must escape the usual fate of being eaten, rotted and scattered. The lucky few are buried quickly — by river mud, volcanic ash or drifting sand — before scavengers and bacteria finish their work. Burial slows decay and starts the long chemistry of preservation.

Over thousands to millions of years, minerals seep into buried bone, shell or wood and harden it to stone, or the remains dissolve away leaving a mould that later fills with sediment. What reaches us is usually the hard parts: shells, teeth, bones. Soft bodies survive only in exceptional deposits.

body.heading: Reading the message carefully
paragraphs: Fossils are not limited to bodies. Footprints, burrows, eggs and even droppings fossilise too, recording behaviour: how an animal walked, grouped, fed. These trace fossils can tell stories that skeletons cannot.

Because fossilisation is so rare and so biased toward hard parts in wet places, the fossil record is a sample, not a census. Whole worlds of soft, small or dry-land life are missing — which makes each well-preserved find a message that very nearly was never sent.

takeaway: Fossils form when remains are buried quickly and turned to stone, preserving rare, precious evidence of past life.
